scenarios.description: General knowledge question — answered, not 'no record'
outputs:
**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) is connection-oriented and reliable. It establishes a connection via a three-way handshake, guarantees delivery, preserves packet ordering, and handles retransmission of lost packets. It also provides flow control and congestion control. The cost is higher latency and overhead.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is connectionless and unreliable by design. It fires datagrams off with no handshake, no delivery guarantee, no ordering, and no retransmission. The cost saving is speed and minimal overhead.

Practical split:

| | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | Required | None |
| Delivery guarantee | Yes | No |
| Ordering | Preserved | Not preserved |
| Header size | 20+ bytes | 8 bytes |
| Typical use | HTTP, SSH, email, file transfer | DNS, VoIP, video streaming, gaming, QUIC |

The rule of thumb: use TCP when every byte must arrive correctly; use UDP when late data is worthless and you'd rather drop it than wait — or when you want to build your own reliability layer on top, as HTTP/3 does with QUIC.

scenarios.description: No hollow opener — no 'Certainly', 'Of course', 'Great question'
outputs:
Continuous integration (CI) is the practice of merging developers' code changes into a shared mainline frequently — typically several times a day — with each merge automatically verified by a build and test run.

The core elements:

- **Shared repository** — everyone works against a single mainline branch rather than long-lived feature branches
- **Automated build** — every commit triggers a build that compiles the code and runs the test suite
- **Fast feedback** — the build should complete quickly enough that breakage is caught within minutes, not days
- **Fix breakage first** — a broken mainline takes priority over new work

The point is to avoid "integration hell": the painful, unpredictable merge effort that accumulates when branches diverge for weeks. Small, frequent integrations make conflicts trivial and defects easy to attribute to a specific change.

CI is usually paired with continuous delivery (CD), which extends the pipeline so that any build passing its tests is automatically deployable to production. Common tooling includes GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, and Buildkite.
